blocks.title: This is the traditional way
blocks.text: This guide shows how traditional farmers usually plant papaya. Use it as a starting point. For a higher yield, update it: plant certified seed or clean planting material, test your soil, and follow the right spacing and fertilizer.

This guide shows how Filipino farmers usually grow papaya from seed in bags, plant it out and care for it until the first ripe fruits, for backyards and small farms. It covers native types as well as Red Lady and other hybrids grown here.

Before you plant, get the field ready with our [land preparation guide for fruit and plantation trees](/land-preparation/fruit-tree-land-preparation). Then choose your seed or planting material with the [papaya nutrient deficiency guide](/nutrient-deficiencies/papaya-nutrient-deficiency). For more on the crop, read [pagtatanim ng puno](/crops/pagtatanim-ng-puno).
When to plant papaya

Many farmers sow seed near the end of the dry season and plant out at the start of the rains, around May to June, so the young plants get steady water. With water on hand papaya can be planted in any month, but planting just before the typhoon months risks broken plants.
What you plant

Seed from a ripe, well shaped fruit of a good bearing tree, washed of its jelly coat and dried in the shade, or bought hybrid seed such as Red Lady. Farmers sow 3 to 4 seeds a bag in loose soil, keep two seedlings a bag and plant out when the seedlings are about 15 cm tall or around 2 months old.
Paano magtanim ng papaya, step by step

Papaya flowers about 3 to 4 months after planting out and the first fruits ripen 4 to 5 months later. The seedling stage before that is about 2 months. The crop is ready about 8 months after planting.
Before planting (Bago magtanim)

items.title: 14 days before planting: Clear the field and dig the holes
items.text: Clear the weeds, loosen the soil and mark the spots about 2.5 m apart each way. Dig holes about 45 cm wide and 45 cm deep, and mix compost or dried manure into the soil that goes back in.

blocks.text: The nursery (Punlaan)

items.title: 2 months before planting: Sow the seeds in bags
items.text: Fill small plastic bags with loose garden soil mixed with compost or rice hull. Sow 3 to 4 seeds a bag about 1 cm deep, water every day and keep the bags in light shade. Tip: Seeds come up in about 15 to 20 days. Old or poorly dried seed comes up slowly.

items.title: 40 days before planting: Thin to two seedlings a bag
items.text: When the seedlings have a few true leaves, cut off the weakest so two are left in each bag. Keep watering every day and move the bags into fuller sun a week before planting out.

blocks.text: Planting day (Pagtatanim)

items.title: Planting day: Plant out the seedlings
items.text: Cut the bag away without breaking the soil and set the seedlings in the hole at the same depth they grew. Press the soil, water well and make a small mound so rain does not pool around the stem. Tip: Papaya dies fast in standing water, so plant on a raised spot or a ridge in wet ground.

blocks.text: Care while it grows (Pag aalaga)

items.title: Day 1: Water until the plants take hold
items.text: Water the new plants every day for the first week or two, then about once a week in dry weather. Mulch with dried grass to keep the soil moist.

items.title: Day 30: First side dressing
items.text: About a month after planting out, scatter a handful of complete fertilizer (14 14 14) in a ring around each plant and cover it with soil. Many farmers repeat every month or two, adding urea and potash once the plants flower.

items.title: Day 30: Weed by hand around the plants
items.text: Pull or hoe the weeds carefully, since papaya roots stay near the surface. Keep the base clean and mulched.

items.title: Month 2: Watch for ringspot and mites
items.text: Look at the leaves often for yellow mottling, narrow leaves or ring spots on the fruit, and pull out and bury sick plants at once. Check the underside of old leaves for tiny red mites and cut off badly hit leaves. Tip: Do not plant squash, cucumber or watermelon next to papaya, since they share the ringspot virus.

items.title: Month 3: Keep the best plant in each hole
items.text: When the flowers show, about 3 to 4 months after planting out, keep the strongest plant with bisexual or female flowers and cut the others. With native papaya, cut out most of the male trees, the ones with long hanging flower stalks.

items.title: Month 4: Feed the flowering plants
items.text: Once flowering starts, give each plant complete fertilizer with potash every month or two so the fruits fill well. Water weekly in dry spells and earth up the base in the rainy season for drainage.

blocks.text: Harvest (Anihan)

items.title: Month 8: Pick the first fruits
items.text: Pick green fruits for cooking, and for eating pick when yellow streaks show at the tip and the sap is no longer milky. Twist the fruit off by hand or with a pole and keep it from dropping.

blocks.text: Spacing, water and fertilizer for papaya
Spacing
About 2.5 m between plants and between rows. Holes about 45 cm wide and deep. Two seedlings planted a hole, later cut back to the single best plant.
Water

Seedlings in bags are watered every day. After planting out, daily watering until the plants take hold, then about weekly in dry months. In the rainy season the base is mounded or the rows ridged so water drains away, since standing water kills papaya quickly.
Fertilizer

Compost or dried manure mixed into the hole. A handful of complete fertilizer (14 14 14) about a month after planting out, then every month or two. Once the plants flower, many farmers add urea (46 0 0) and muriate of potash (0 0 60) or keep giving complete fertilizer so the fruits fill. Seedlings in bags sometimes get a pinch of urea every two weeks. To read what a bag really gives, see our guide to [fertilizer for this crop](/blog/fertilizer-for-fruit-trees).
Care and harvest
Care while it grows

Hand weeding and mulching, careful not to cut the shallow roots. Cutting extra plants and most male trees once the flowers show. Taking off old yellow leaves. Pulling and burying plants with ringspot. Mounding the base in the rainy season, and in windy places some farmers bend or prop young plants against typhoons.
When and how to harvest

Flowers come about 3 to 4 months after planting out and fruit is ready 4 to 5 months later. Green fruit is picked for cooking. For eating, fruit is picked when yellow first shows at the tip and the sap turns clear, then ripened in the shade. Fruits are handled gently and never allowed to fall. A papaya stand bears well until about its third or fourth year.
Common mistakes when planting papaya

items: Planting in low, wet ground where the roots rot after heavy rain.
Saving seed from a sick or poor tree, which passes on weak plants.
Planting next to squash, cucumber or watermelon, which spreads ringspot.
Leaving every seedling in the hole and every male tree standing.
Hoeing deep near the trunk and cutting the shallow roots.
Leaving sick plants in the field, so the virus spreads to the rest.

blocks.text: How to get a higher yield of papaya
The traditional way gets a crop, but small changes add up. These are the first things to change, one season at a time.

items: Use clean seed of a tolerant variety from a trusted seed company or a healthy mother tree.
Test the soil and feed by the result, with enough potash and lime where soil is sour.
Plant on ridges or mounds with drainage canals for the rainy season.
Scout every week for ringspot, mites and mealybugs and remove sick plants at once.
Water regularly in dry months and mulch for steady fruiting.
Plant a new block every year or two, since old stands lose vigor and catch disease.
